subject: Acme discovery: competitive checklist, SLA questions & next tests
messages:
From: Rachel Kim <rachel.kim@redwood.ai>
To: Amy Collins <amy.collins@acme.com>
Cc: Samir Patel <samir.patel@acme.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 15:08:00 -0800
Subject: Recap + next steps from today's call (competitive items + SLAs)

Hi Amy / Samir,

Thanks again for carving out time today — appreciated the candidness on evaluation criteria. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps so we stay aligned: 

1) Primary evaluation goals you mentioned:
- Predictable p99 latency under 100ms for short prompts (~128 tokens).
- Consistent per-token cost and a clear path to reduce unit cost using batching/quantization.
- Strong incident response SLA (RCA within 72 hours for Sev1) and a runbook for cascading failures.

2) Where Redwood landed in the call as differentiators:
- Unified API across hosted/dedicated/private so you can prototype on hosted and then pin to private for isolation.
- Cost controls (batching + cache + quantization profiles) with observable token-level billing.
- Smart routing and graceful fallbacks — in the event of capacity pressure we can route to a compatible variant automatically (this was top-of-mind given your multi-region needs).

3) Competitive items you asked us to validate:
- Incident behavior and support SLAs vs hyperscaler-managed inference endpoints (GCP/other).
- How RCA cadence and transparency differ during multi-hour incidents.
- What concrete tests you can run to compare live behavior under spike / degraded capacity.

Proposed next steps: 
A) I attached a short one-pager comparing Redwood vs typical hyperscaler inference endpoints (redwood-vs-hyperscalers-one-pager.pdf) — highlights incident response flows and fallback semantics.
B) Technical test plan: Jordan from our pre-sales team will propose 2 smoke tests + 1 stress test you can run in a day:
   - Latency conformance (128-token p50/p95/p99 under production payload)
   - Failover test (simulate node OOM and observe fallback path + end-to-end latency degradation)
   - Spike test (burst traffic 3x baseline for 10 minutes to observe autoscale/burst behavior)
C) SLA discussion: Marcus (CS/ops) will send our standard Sev matrix and a sample RCA template so you can compare to GCP's published incident notes.

Can we tentatively schedule the tests next week? Jordan, Marcus — can you confirm availability Wed/Thu (Feb 18/19) for a 30–45m session?

Amy — any other must-have checks you want included in the plan?

Thanks,

Rachel Kim
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
T: +1 415 555 0123

Attachment: redwood-vs-hyperscalers-one-pager.pdf

Subject: Re: Recap + next steps from today's call (competitive items + SLAs)

Thanks Rachel — useful summary. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 

- On incident SLAs: our security team requires an RCA within 72 hours for Sev1 and daily status updates until resolved. We also ask for a post-incident timeline and mitigation steps. How frequently does Redwood provide an initial incident summary?
- On failover: in prior tests with a hyperscaler managed endpoint we saw a 6–8s tail latency spike during failover windows — we want to validate that fallback doesn't amplify tail latencies for short prompts.
- Can you provide an anonymized example RCA or timeline for a recent Sev1 incident? GCP rep — curious if you have a public incident timeline we can look at for comparison.

Also Samir and I are available Thu Feb 18 morning for the smoke tests. We prefer the failover test first.

Best,
Amy
Amy Collins
Head of AI Platforms | Acme Corp

Subject: RE: Recap + next steps from today's call (competitive items + SLAs)

Hi Amy / Samir — Jordan from pre-sales here. Thanks for the availability. Short note with the concrete test plan and what we'll need from Acme to run them quickly: 

Planned tests (ordered for the session you requested):
1) Failover validation (30 mins) — objective: confirm graceful fallback without p99 amplification for short prompts. Steps: warm a small pool, then trigger a forced worker drain; measure p50/p95/p99 and error rate. What we need: a representative 128-token prompt set (10–20 prompts) and a short client that can emit steady traffic at 50 rps. 
2) Latency conformance (20 mins) — objective: p50/p95/p99 at target throughput. Steps: run a 5-minute stable load at expected QPS. Need: baseline QPS numbers and model variant to pin.
3) Spike test (10–15 mins) — cause a 3x burst to verify autoscale and any transient errors.

Artifacts we'll share during the session:
- Real-time dashboard link, token-level cost estimates, and a short incident playbook note (we'll also drop the incident-sla-matrix.xlsx in the Drive after this email).

RCA example: since you asked for an anonymized Sev1 timeline, attaching a redacted RCA summary that shows initial detection, mitigation steps, timeframe to restoration, and a one-paragraph postmortem. Note that hyperscaler-managed incidents sometimes have longer RCA publication windows because they require cross-team signoff; we can point to specific public incident bulletins on their status pages if you want those for comparison.

Amy — you asked how often we produce an initial incident summary: for Sev1 we aim to produce an initial incident status within 1 hour of detection and a draft RCA within 72 hours. We send daily status updates until mitigation is complete. I'll let Marcus add any operational details.

Jordan Blake
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Attachment: incident-sla-matrix.xlsx

From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>

Date: Mon, 16 Feb 2026 11:22:00 -0800
Subject: RE: Recap + next steps from today's call (competitive items + SLAs)

Hi Amy / Samir — Marcus from CS/ops here. A few operational notes ahead of Thu's session and a quick comparison to typical hyperscaler behavior so you have concrete expectations: 

- Incident cadence: Redwood initial summary within 1 hour (automated alert + on-call triage), interim updates every 8–12 hours for extended incidents, and a targeted RCA draft within 72 hours. We can accelerate update frequency during an active critical incident if you require hourly updates via a dedicated channel.
- RCA contents: timeline, root cause hypothesis, immediate mitigations, long-term remediation plan, affected customers (anonymized), and lessons learned. Attached is a redacted RCA example we use internally and share in postmortems.

Hyperscaler differences (practical notes):
- Hyperscalers often provide status page entries early but the formal RCA can take weeks due to cross-org sign-offs. That can be a blocker for customers wanting fast post-incident mitigation changes.
- Managed endpoints on hyperscalers may revert to broader default autoscaling policies during platform maintenance — meaning your app could see elevated p99s while the endpoint scales up. Our routing + fallback approach aims to avoid that by allowing an alternative compatible model variant with lower memory footprint to pick up load quickly.

Proposed SLA items for the commercial contract draft (high level):
- Sev1: initial summary within 1 hour, daily updates until mitigation, draft RCA within 72 hours.
- Sev2: initial summary within 4 hours, RCA within 10 business days.
- Credits: reasonable service credit model tied to p99 latency SLA breaches and sustained error rates.

Next steps: we will run the failover test first on Thu 18 Feb 09:00 PT. Jordan will share the Drive link and gRPC/HTTP test harness. Rachel — can you confirm the calendar invite and include the Drive link? Amy / Samir — please upload the 128-token sample prompts and a short README with expected QPS by EOD Wed so we can pre-warm.

If you'd like, I can also provide a short side-by-side table after tests showing measurable differences (p99 behavior, time-to-fallback, RCA lag) — that tends to be helpful for procurement.

Thanks,
Marcus Lin
Director, Customer Reliability | Redwood Inference
